neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration: absent at great toes bilaterally, severely reduced at ankles (0 seconds), reduced at knees (4 seconds). Proprioception: absent at great toes bilaterally, severely reduced at ankles. Light touch mildly reduced in feet bilaterally. Pinprick relatively preserved in feet. neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 1+ bilaterally. Patellar absent bilaterally. Achilles absent bilaterally. Brachioradialis trace bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Severe dysmetria on finger-nose bilaterally — PSEUDOATHETOSIS of outstretched hands with eyes closed. Positive Romberg (falls within 5 seconds of eye closure). Heel-shin moderately impaired bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based ataxic gait. Stomping quality to steps. Falls in tandem walk. Dramatically worsens with eye closure (sensory ataxia).
neurological_exam.special_tests: Pseudoathetosis present (hands move involuntarily with eyes closed). No Babinski. No clonus. Lhermitte's sign negative.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive sensory loss and imbalance over 2 years, ataxic gait, no pain
patient.history_present_illness: Patricia Osei is a 63-year-old retired administrative director presenting with a 2-year history of progressive gait instability and sensory changes in her feet and hands. Unlike many neuropathy presentations, she has minimal pain — her predominant complaint is a profound sense of unsteadiness that she likens to 'walking on a cushion of air.' She has had two significant falls in the past 6 months, both in the dark or when closing her eyes in the shower. She has noticed increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks including fastening buttons and picking up small objects, with a sense of losing track of where her fingers are without looking. Her balance is dramatically worse with eyes closed than open, and she uses a cane now. She was evaluated for inner ear problems twice — hearing is normal, and an ear specialist found no vestibular disorder. Her past medical history is notable for a 12-year history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.8%) and a seronegative (anti-SSA/SSB negative) dry eye syndrome she has managed with artificial tears for 8 years. Neurological review of prior records reveals that previous neurologists noted reduced reflexes and attributed findings to diabetes, but the predominance of deep sensory loss and sensory ataxia over pain is considered atypical for typical diabetic neuropathy.

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — sensory neuronopathy pattern. Sensory nerve action potentials severely reduced or absent in both upper and lower extremities in a non-length-dependent, pan-extremity distribution. Motor nerve conduction studies normal. Needle EMG: no fibrillations, no chronic reinnervation changes. Findings localize to a disorder affecting sensory neurons above the level of the peripheral nerve, consistent with a sensory ganglionopathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Sjögren's syndrome sensory neuronopathy (dorsal root ganglionopathy)
critical_actions: Recognize sensory neuronopathy pattern — non-length-dependent pan-sensory loss with normal motor NCS is DRG localization, not peripheral nerve
Order anti-SSA/SSB — even patients with prior negative results can seroconvert over time
Lip biopsy to confirm Sjögren's before treating with IVIG or hydroxychloroquine
Check paraneoplastic panel (anti-Hu) to exclude malignant etiology — urgent if positive
Do not attribute to B12 deficiency or diabetes without confirming that B12 normalization improves symptoms
MRI spine to exclude posterior column disease (B12 SCDC differential)
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose as pure diabetic neuropathy — non-length-dependent pattern with absent motor NCS and pseudoathetosis is not diabetic
Do not stop metformin reflexively — B12 low-normal is addressable with supplementation while continuing metformin
Do not attribute to vestibular disease — vestibular testing was already negative; this is proprioceptive ataxia from DRG involvement
Do not delay IVIG while awaiting all test results in patient with rapidly progressing sensory ataxia and falls

differential.key_features: Diabetic neuropathy is length-dependent — distal > proximal; PAIN is dominant; motor NCS mildly affected; proprioception and vibration loss in isolation with absent SNAPs pan-extremity is NOT diabetic pattern
B12 284 pg/mL low-normal, MMA equivocal; MRI spine shows NO posterior column signal change; B12 normalization did not improve symptoms — B12 was NOT the primary cause

differential.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy (anti-Hu, small cell lung cancer)
differential.key_features: Anti-Hu negative, anti-Yo/CV2 negative; anti-SSA positive with Sjögren's confirmed by lip biopsy; non-smoker; age-appropriate cancer screening current
Anti-SSA positive and lip biopsy confirmatory — not idiopathic

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: Chronic dry eye + diabetes creates anchoring toward routine metabolic neuropathy; sensory ataxia pattern is the key diagnostic clue
PSEUDOATHETOSIS is pathognomonic for severe proprioceptive loss (DRG) — not seen in typical diabetic or B12 neuropathy
Sjögren's seroconversion: anti-SSA can become positive over years; prior negative does not exclude current Sjögren's — must re-test
KEY NCS PATTERN: Absent SNAPs pan-extremity (both upper and lower, not length-dependent) with NORMAL motor NCS and NORMAL EMG = sensory neuronopathy above DRG
B12 supplementation trial is both diagnostic (no improvement = not B12) and therapeutic (addresses metformin-related insufficiency)
IVIG for Sjögren's ganglionopathy is stabilization therapy — DRG neurons lost to ganglionitis do not regenerate; early treatment prevents further loss
Paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy (anti-Hu) is critical to exclude — has different treatment implications and underlying malignancy
